articles.text: The Piedmont City Council accepted a $748,000 grant for the Moraga Avenue Pedestrian Safety Project at their Monday, August 18 Council meeting. The project will include the installation of bulb-outs, flashing beacons, and other pedestrian and bike improvements at four intersections along Moraga Avenue. Both the 2014 Piedmont Bike/ Pedestrian Master Plan and the 2021 Safer Streets Plan recommended pedestrian safety improvements to the following intersections on Moraga Ave. • Ramona Ave. • Highland Ave. • Mesa Ave. • Red Rock Rd. The improvements also include a proposed “No right turn on Red” sign from Moraga onto Highland, heading uphill. This follows complaints from cyclists about cars at the intersection. The City applied for the grant last fall with the Alameda County Transportation Commission (ACTC). Council approved a resolution of support for staff to file the application on October 7, 2024.

articles.text: Kiran Bawa working at her desk in City Hall. Now back at work for the City of Piedmont, Finance Director Kiran Bawa has been adjusting well to work in the California weather. With over two decades of public sector finance experience, Bawa began her service with the City on July 2, 2025. As Finance Director, Bawa oversees citywide finance functions, including accounting, payroll, auditing, purchasing, investments, and the development of the City’s annual budget. Bawa is taking over after the retirement of Finance Director Mike Szczech. The appointment marks a return to Piedmont for Bawa, who previously served as Piedmont’s Finance Director from 2016-2017. articles.text: All businesses operating in Piedmont – including home-based operations, independent contractors, consultants, freelancers, online storefronts – are required to obtain a City business license. Businesses currently operating without a required license may soon receive a letter providing information about how to register and pay applicable taxes. Businesses that have not previously registered may be responsible for back taxes for the last three years. However, penalties typically associated with late registration will be waived if businesses register and pay within 90 days from the date on their notification letter. Business owners can now register and pay applicable taxes quickly and easily through a new online system at piedmont. hdlgov.com. Support is available through a dedicated customer support line at (510) 250-1975, with experts available to guide business owners through the registration process and help calculate taxes based on individual business structures. Businesses requiring a license include: • Home-based businesses (includes 1099 self-employment) • Online storefronts or “influencers” with a Piedmont business address • Landlords operating long- • term or short-term rentals Contractors and consultants working in Piedmont, even if located elsewhere Notification letters to unregistered businesses are part of the compliance audit recommended by the City’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee. The audit follows a public education campaign conducted earlier this year to raise awareness of existing laws among community members. Businesses that need assistance or have questions about their registration status can contact customer support at (510) 250-1975 or visit piedmont. ca.gov/ComplianceLetter. With the pool project projected to come to a close this month, Bawa addressed concerns of the pool’s perceived cost overrun. “The cost did go up, but not any more than [the City] can handle,” said Bawa. “With the Measure UU funds and the contributions and the grants that we have received, the pool is slated to finish within the budget.” The pool project was initially approved for a bond of $19.5 million through Measure UU. The total cost budget of the pool is now $34.9 million. With the budget for City projects racing into the tens of millions, managing Piedmont’s Finances is difficult, highly detailed work. Luckily, Bawa is no stranger to managing bonds. Among her achievements while working in Virginia Bawa was credited with architecting the bond referendum to finance a new $120 million high school, maintaining the City’s AAA bond ratings, and helping to craft a revenue sharing agreement between the government and the schools. Bawa believes that the most important traits for a Finance Manager are accountability, integrity, job knowledge, teamwork and collaboration. She also stresses the importance of longterm financial stability and proper infrastructure maintenance. “Finance is such a field that it doesn’t flow naturally to a lot of people – and it’s very crucial in making decisions,” said Bawa. She is an American Pit Bull Terrier mix weighing 34 pounds who staff describe as full of happy-golucky energy and personality. Macarena is sweet, friendly, and just a little goofy. This puppy loves other dogs and plays well in group settings, especially when there’s a game of chase involved. She knows sit and down and loves playing fetch. On a recent field trip, the volunteer walker reported she rode well in the car and was a joy on the walks. Macarena’s working on keeping all four paws on the ground when greeting people, so she’d do best in a home without small kids for now. She is affectionate, curious, and full of love. She studied Economics at Mills College and her parents’ work sparked a passion for civil service. “I knew my heart was there – the community interface, giving back to the community,” said Bawa. “...I just like where the rubber meets the road, the passion of improving people’s lives.” With her youngest child transitioning toward college, Bawa’s family is looking at colleges in California’s UC system for higher education. She is also excited to see construction finish on the Community Pool Project, having grown up in swimming sports herself. With the pool project projected to come to a close this month, Bawa addressed concerns of the pool’s perceived cost overrun. “The cost did go up, but not any more than [the City] can handle,” said Bawa. “With the Measure UU funds and the contributions and the grants that we have received, the pool is slated to finish within the budget.” The pool project was initially approved for a bond of $19.5 million through Measure UU. The total cost budget of the pool is now $34.9 million. With the budget for City projects racing into the tens of millions, managing Piedmont’s Finances is difficult, highly detailed work. Luckily, Bawa is no stranger to managing bonds. Among her achievements while working in Virginia Bawa was credited with architecting the bond referendum to finance a new $120 million high school, maintaining the City’s AAA bond ratings, and helping to craft a revenue sharing agreement between the government and the schools. Bawa believes that the most important traits for a Finance Manager are accountability, integrity, job knowledge, teamwork and collaboration. She also stresses the importance of longterm financial stability and proper infrastructure maintenance. “Finance is such a field that it doesn’t flow naturally to a lot of people – and it’s very crucial in making decisions,” said Bawa. She recounts long hours in the past, working sometimes until 3 a.m. with Council Members and Committees during her time with the City of Oakland.

Residents can read the draft LHMP online at piedmont.ca.gov/ LHMP and submit comments online at https://communityfeedback.opengov.com/portals/piedmontca/Issue_14549 or by email to LHMP@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: On Aug. 27, 2025, the Beacon Grand Hotel will host Elegance Meets Impact, a fashion show and auction benefiting George Mark Children’s House. Legendary designer Lily Samii, known for dressing senators, royals and Hollywood stars, will step out of retirement for the one-night-only event. Samii will present 20 gowns from her private collection, each selected for the show and auction. “I thought my days of runway shows were behind me, but the children of George Mark called me back,” Samii said. “Each gown I’ve chosen carries a piece of my heart. If my work can bring comfort and care to even one child, then it is worth every moment out of retirement.” Founded more than 20 years ago, George Mark Children’s House is the first freestanding pediatric palliative care center in the United States. It provides respite, end-of-life care and family support in a setting that blends the warmth of home with hospital-level expertise. Parents are given space to rest, siblings receive counseling, and children take part in art, music and play therapy. Guests at Elegance Meets Impact will see San Francisco leaders, philanthropists and community figures walk the runway in Samii’s designs. A raffle will also award two United Airlines Premium Economy roundtrip tickets to Europe, valued at $17,000. Proceeds from the evening will go directly to compassionate care for children and families. That includes medical support, grief counseling, meals, overnights for parents and programs that focus on quality of life. The impact of support from Lily Samii will participate in a one-night-only fashion show and auction benefiting George Mark Children’s House on August 27. the event will be felt directly at George Mark Children’s House. Funds raised will help provide respite care so parents can rest while children receive expert medical support, end-of-life care in a home-like setting, bereavement and grief counseling for families and siblings, play and art therapy that give children joy and connection, and comprehensive family support such as meals and overnight stays. The event itself will take place Wednesday, Aug. 27, 2025, at the Beacon Grand Hotel in San Francisco’s Union Square. A VIP reception begins at 5:30 p.m., followed by general admission at 6 p.m. Seating is limited, and tickets can be reserved at georgemark.org/elegance-meets-impact.

articles.text: Piedmont High School began the 2025–26 school year with notable changes on campus, namely a newly implemented ban on cell phones during class. Students are no longer able to access their phones at school, excluding lunch time, a change that students are still adjusting to. With last year’s seniors having graduated, the halls feel different without the Class of 2025’s familiar presence. On the first day, seniors and freshmen were celebrated with donut holes before going to their first classes. As always, the shift from summer break to textbooks, long classes, and lectures feels jarring for both teachers and students, but over the first week, a sense of cohesion among the student body has begun to take shape. The week ended with a schoolwide assembly, which included introductions of Dr. David Yoshihara, the principal, and Joseph Marik, the assistant principal, and the ASB representatives for the year. Dr. Yoshihara has also announced the continuation of the Highlander Hunt and a surprising new addition to PHS school spirit – our new mascot in the form of a purple and gold lion. Students found the mascot walking around and greeting them at the front door. The school is currently looking for suggestions of a name for the new mascot. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School and an intern writer with the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: On August 19 Chabot Space & Science Center marked a remarkable milestone – 25 years atop Oakland’s Skyline Boulevard. Perched amid the largest stand of coastal redwoods in the East Bay, the nonprofit Center has become a hub for hands-on space and science learning, community engagement, and cosmic inspiration. The journey to Skyline began long before the current facility opened its doors in 2000. Founded in 1883 as an astronomical observatory in Oakland, Chabot has a 142-year legacy of inspiring curiosity about the universe. Its move to its current 13-acre site in Redwood Regional Park allowed the institution to expand its vision: a science center that connects learners of all ages to the wonders of space and our planet. When the new Chabot Space & Science Center opened on August 19, 2000, visitors encountered two historic refracting telescopes—Leah (1883) and Rachel (1916)—alongside a full-dome planetarium, classrooms, and interactive exhibits. In 2003, the 36-inch reflecting telescope called Nellie joined the sky-watching family, making Chabot home to the largest public observatory complex in the Western United States. These telescopes have not only delighted amateur astronomers but also contributed to research, including Near Earth Object studies and even relaying information to NASA during the Apollo 13 descent. Over the past quarter century, Chabot has expanded both its facilities and its reach. In 2005, new classrooms and teacher preparation spaces opened with Measure G funding. In 2008, the Center celebrated its 125th anniversary with a year of public programs, and in 2018, Measure WW funded the Observation Deck expansion that added 3,200 square feet of outdoor viewing space. Chabot’s mission has always been to make science and space accessible to all. Today, the center offers a vibrant mix of planetarium shows, workshops, tinkering spaces, lectures, community events, and school programs. Its education team partners closely with Oakland and Contra Costa County schools, emphasizing inquiry-based learning, inclusion, and collaboration—fostering the critical thinking skills essential for the 21st-century workforce. In 2021, a groundbreaking partnership with NASA Ames Research Center brought the NASA Ames Visitor Center to Chabot, complete with hands-on activities, mission artifacts, and exhibits on cutting-edge research. This collaboration also laid the groundwork for the Oakland Space Academy, a workforce development pathway for local youth. As Chabot heads into the rest of 2025 and beyond, the focus is on deepening connections with the community. “Times of transition can be powerful and catalytic moments,” said Adam Tobin, Executive Director and CEO. “When I consider these milestones, reflecting on all that we have accomplished and the impact that we have had, I firmly believe that Chabot’s best days are still to come. In so many ways, Chabot is as well positioned as we have ever been to fulfill our dream of making science inspiring, accessible, and empowering for all.” To celebrate its 25th anniversary on Skyline Boulevard, Chabot will offer programs, events, and activities designed to engage the community, build relationships, and give back to the people of the area that have supported it for the past quarter century. From its 19th-century beginnings to its 21st-century innovations, Chabot remains committed to a simple yet profound mission: to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the Universe and Planet Earth. As the next chapter begins, the view from Skyline has never looked brighter. We hope you’ll join us up on the hill as we celebrate the next 25 years and all that is to come. For more information about Chabot Space and Science Center, 510-336-7300 or go to our website at chabotspace.org. articles.text: Beach 4th grade teacher Ben Spencer offers after-school enrichment class on Mondays Blacktops & Books students play a real-life version of Hungry, Hungry Hippos. Beach Elementary School 4th grade teacher Ben Spencer is offering an after-school enrichment class, Blacktops & Books, for 3rd-5th grade students. The class begins with 50 minutes of high-energy outdoor games and activities and then moves inside for another 50 minutes, where students will complete their homework and participate in academic activities and games. “Parents can expect their kids to have a unique, fun, and academic experience when they participate in Blacktops & Books,” said Spencer. “I’m most looking forward to the kids having fun, developing a love for playing games, and making lifelong, meaningful friendships.” Kids will get a chance to have exercise and will be given an opportunity to get a majority of their weekly homework finished. “Students really benefit from being in a class that is made up of 3rd, 4th, and 5th graders. They all learn from each other. The older ones learn to be leaders and mentors. They also learn how to be patient. The younger kiddos learn valuable social skills and are able to gain a lot of academic confidence because they get support from the older students at Beach. It’s a win-win,” said Spencer. Spencer, who also is the Piedmont High School boys’ basketball coach, and has a knack for making academic work fun and organizing the most fun of outdoor, athletic activities. Enrollment is now open for Blacktops & Books. The first class begins at 3:10 p.m. on Monday, September 8 and the program runs through Monday, November 17. Parents can also sign up their kids for just the first hour of outdoor activities at a discounted price. Visit Homeroom.com/activities/63276 to enroll or email bspencer@piedmont.k12.ca.us. Students are shown playing Banana Tag at Beach School.

articles.text: Samantha Pell recently completed the requirements to be an Eagle Scout. She is a member of Piedmont’s Troop 1, and currently is studying in England for her high school sophomore year. Her Eagle Project was a mural of the Earth at Thornhill Elementary School in Montclair, surrounded by handprints of the outgoing fifth grade class. The mural occupies a wall that has been left empty for the past 10+ years. It surrounds one of the main gardens, adjacent to the playground. What was once a gaping hole in the vibrant and lush environment has now been transformed into a part of the overall environment, adding joy and engagement to the space. Additionally, my dedication serves to encourage the graduating class to return even after they leave, to care for the garden that they are now connected to on another level. On another note, the mural also serves to be a catalyst to Thornhill’s extensive environmental and sustainability programs which greatly benefit the Troop 1 Eagle Scout Samantha Pell K-5 children. This includes the school wide gardening classes taught by Alexis Lavine-Moore with whom Samantha worked on the mural. “It was my goal to help the garden become an even more special space for students, like the garden during my time at Havens Elementary School,” Pell added. articles.text: Kids are back to school, and student-athletes are getting back into their groove ahead of the upcoming fall sports season. Piedmont High will field nine teams for the fall season with both cross-country teams, girls’ volleyball, girls’ tennis, football, flag football, girls’ golf, and both water polo teams. Here’s a look at three key athletes for the upcoming season. JIMMY LAGIOS Football Jimmy Lagios continues a new family tradition, inheriting Piedmont High’s varsity football team’s starting quarterback role from his brother, Markos, who graduated earlier this year. He’ll wear the same No. 4. In addition to playing the junior varsity football team as a freshman, Lagios earned starting minutes on the varsity boys’ soccer team and varsity baseball team. We named Lagios our honorable mention for our 2025 Freshman of the Year award for his contributions to the boys’ soccer team reaching the D4 NCS Final as the top seed and winning the D5 CIF NorCal championship with the No. 5 seed as a freshman starter. Lagios was credited with three assists and one goal as a key cog in coach Ben Russell’s central midfield. He logged one of his assists in Piedmont’s 4-2 win over No. 9 Urban in NCS, helping give his team a 2-1 lead when laying off a pass to Logan Faucher. He scored his lone goal on a header in a 3-1 Staff Photos Jimmy Lagios is set to be the football team’s starting quarterback as a sophomore. win over Hayward during the regular season. Soccer finished its season with a 13-4-9 (W-T-L) record. In baseball, Lagios had two appearances as a pitcher and struck out five batters. LEIGHTON MAND Cross Country Leighton Mand is entering her third year as a varsity runner for the cross country team. She earned out 2025 Sophomore of the Year award and was our honorable mention for 2024 Freshman of the Year. She was our Athlete of the Month in November and our honorable mention for October. Mand reached the CIF State Cross Country Championship last year, where she finished 74th of 201 athletes with a time of 19:52.7. At the NCS Championship, Mand placed sixth of 127 runners to qualify for State. She also finished fifth out of 40 runners at the WACC Championship in 19:16.8. She is a distance runner on the track team in the spring. Last season, Mand reached the NCS Meet of Champions in the 1600 meters and was a member of the 4x800 relay team. In the 1600, Leighton finished the season 17th of 24 at the Meet of Champions with a time of 5:23.46. To get there, she was sixth of 23 at the NCS Bayshore Championship in 5:24.42, while she finished fourth of 37 at the WACC Championship in 5:25.80. On the 4x800 team alongside Nikita Gorelik, Skylar Best, and Caroline Taylor, the team finished 12th of 16 at the Meet of Champions with a time of 10:07.23. They also placed third of 11 teams at the League meet Bayshore in 10:13.46. LUKE MCAULIFFE Water Polo Luke McAuliffe is entering his third year as the Highlanders’ starting goalie this fall. We named him the Post’s 2024 Sophomore of the Year after he helped lead the school to its first-ever North Coast Section championship. Last season, PHS finished 16-10 and reached the Division 2 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 4 seed. They lost a heated 14-11 game to No. 5 Washington in NCS, but bashed No. 13 Freedom 17-9 in the opening round. In 2023 as a sophomore McAuliffe was instrumental in the school’s only NCS title. As the No. 4 seed PHS beat No. 5 Newark Memorial 12-9 in the quarterfinals, upset No. 1 Marin Academy 13-9 in the semifinals, and defeated league rival No. 3 Alameda 10-8 for the championship. RAVI SILVERBERG Basketball Piedmont High Class of 2025 Macalester College Class of 2029 Ravi Silverberg graduated from Piedmont High with the Class of 2025 after leading the basketball team to the North Coast Section title game as the squad’s leading scorer. He was the Post’s Athlete of the Month in January and February. In the post-season Silverberg scored 18 points in Piedmont’s 87-49 win over Ukiah in the first round, scored 25 points in their 78-69 quarterfinals finals win over Bethel—scoring his 1,000th career point in the process. He scored 17 points in their semifinals’ 60-53 win over Windsor and finished with 33 points in the Highlanders’ 75-70 loss to St. Patrick in the championship game. He also scored 18 points in PHS’ 84-71 loss to Natomas in the D4 CIF State first round. Ravi details his workout regimen ahead of his freshman season on Macalester College’s basketball team. What was your workout program this summer? This summer, my routine included weightlifting five times a week and playing basketball every day. I’ve been especially focused on getting a high volume of shots up during each session in the gym. What were your fitness goals for the summer? My main goals were to build strength, improve my athleticism, and become more consistent with my shooting. I’ve been working on extending my range and becoming more fluid shooting three-pointers off the dribble. How are you measuring your development? I track my progress by gradually increasing the difficulty of my workouts. Each week, I challenge myself with more advanced drills to push my limits and see growth. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I usually train with teammates and friends. I also apply techniques and guidance I’ve received from previous coaches, adapting them to create a personalized routine that suits me best. What was a recent milestone that you accomplished? A recent milestone was bench pressing 225 pounds which is something I’ve been working toward for a long time. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Half the battle is just showing up. Always be confident and trust the work you put in. We have a great year planned ahead, with many opportunities for our community to come together to discuss topics of focus for our district. articles.text: As children return to school this fall, singers with the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) are preparing for another season of music, joy and community. Children ages 5 to 18 can discover their voices, build confidence and make lasting friendships at PEBCC. The youngest singers, in Kinder Choir, are introduced to choral music in a nurturing and playful environment. In the Training Department, students learn fundamentals such as pitch, tempo, rhythm and phrasing. A typical rehearsal includes vocal warmups, group repertoire, music theory, vocal games and choreography. Singers learn how to blend with others while developing their musicianship. forming Department, students are ready for the highest level of children’s choral training. They take on advanced repertoire, sharpen stage presence and prepare for performances and collaborations in the Bay Area and beyond. Besides weekly rehearsals, students experience music through summer camps, workshops, combined rehearsals and collaborations with other choirs. Performing Department members serve as ambassadors for the Choir and the East Bay through local concerts, professional partnerships and appearances at international festivals. Two advanced choirs tour domestically and abroad each year, with recent trips to Finland, Estonia, England and Canada. In 2024, PEBCC won first prize at the Llangollen International Eisteddfod in Wales, earning the title “Young Choir of the World.” Tours often include homestays with local families, giving singers a chance to immerse themselves in a different culture. PEBCC also hosts the Golden Gate International Choral Festival every three years. The festival will return in July 2026, bringing choirs from around the world for a week of workshops, concerts and shared musical experiences. Every rehearsal at PEBCC is about learning, exploring and connecting. Singers grow through each level of the program, building skills, confidence and musical understanding along the way. Classes meet once or twice a week, with multiple schedule options to fit families’ needs. PEBCC is enrolling now for the 2025–26 season. articles.text: Marin Theatre Company (MTC) premieres Jonathan Spector’s Eureka Day on August 28, featuring nearly all its original cast members from the 2018 world premiere. The play is set at the Eureka Day School in Berkeley, California, portrayed as a “bastion of progressive ideals with a board of directors that values inclusion above all else.” The majority of the play takes place during meetings between parents and administrators concerning requirements for vaccination after an outbreak of mumps at the school. These meetings prompt school leadership to reconsider its liberal vaccine policy in comedic and dramatic ways. MTC’s production of Eureka Day is presented in partnership with Aurora Theatre Company, where the play had its world premiere in 2018, two years before the COVID-19 pandemic and the discourse over required vaccinations that followed. The New York Playwright Jonathan Spector Times called Eureka Day and Jonathan Spector’s “lively portrait of a debate over mandatory vaccinations” and “the perfect play for our age of disagreement.” An opening night post-show reception will be held on Tuesday, September 2. A pre-show presentation from MTC’s stage designer is held on Thursday, September 18. Eureka Day is appropriate for audience members 14 and older. Visit https://purchase.marintheatre.org/EventAvailability?EventId=49801 to purchase tickets.

articles.text: SFJAZZ opens its 2025- 26 season, curated by Executive Artistic Director Terence Blanchard, on September 4. Keyboard master, jazz organist and GRAMMY-nominated composer Cory Henry returns to SFJAZZ with his band the Funk Apostles on September 4 and 5, launching the company’s new season. Henry is a former member of Snarky Puppy and toured with many mainstream artists including Bruce Springsteen, Michael McDonald, Boyz II Men, Kenny Garrett, and The Roots. He launched his solo career in 2018 and released his debut single, “Trade It All”, with his band The Funk Apostles. Both Thursday and Friday concerts begin at 7:30 p.m. Henry also appears as a guest musician with the gospel group Blind Boys of Alabama on September 6 and 7. The nine-month season features over 350 concerts and includes performances by jazz luminaries as well as emerging young voices shaping the genre’s future. This season also marks the return of last year’s successful emerging artists series entitled “The Upswing,” producing a new class of Resident Artistic Directors which include Michael League, Meshell Ndegeocello, Omar Sosa and Immanuel Wilkins. Visit www.sfjazz.org/tickets/ productions/25-26/cory-henryfunk-apostles/ to purchase tickets. Cory Henry

articles.text: Pianist Yuja Wang opens 2025-26 season The San Francisco Symphony begins its 2025-26 season with its annual opening gala on September 12, featuring pianist Yuja Wang and Seoul Philharmonic conductor Jaap van Zweden. The evening’s program features Piotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky’s Piano Concerto No. 1, John Adams’s Short Ride in a Fast Machine, and Ottorino Respighi’s Pines of Rome. The company’s opening gala concert is one of three programs Zweden conducts with the San Francisco Symphony this season. Wang, a renowned Chinese-born classical pianist from Beijing, made her San Francisco Symphony debut in 2006 and toured Asia with the company and its former conductor Michael Tilson Thomas in November 2012. She has since become a recurring guest pianist at Davies Symphony Hall and has performed with the Berlin Philharmonic, Oslo Philharmonic, Toronto Symphony Orchestra and more. Guests are invited to a complimentary preconcert reception featuring a celebratory toast, light bites, and entertainment in the orchestra lobby from 5:30 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. Specialty cocktails are available for purchase at the orchestra level bar following the gala concert until 9:30 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2025-26/Opening-Gala. American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) premieres Playwright Ins Choi’s award-winning comedy-drama, Kim’s Convenience, opening Thursday, September 18. The play is based on Choi’s experiences working at his own family’s convenience store, Kim’s Grocer, in Scarborough, Toronto, and follows family patriarch Mr. Kim as he faces a changing neighborhood landscape and the gap between his values and those of his Canadian-born children. Choi called the play a “love letter to his parents and to all first-generation immigrants who call Canada their home.” Kim’s Convenience debuted on July 6, 2011 at the Toronto Fringe Festival to wide critical acclaim and inspired a popular Netflix series of the same name. “I’m very excited about bringing this production to A.C.T.,” said Choi. “Some of my nieces and nephews live in the Bay Area and have never seen me perform or this play which was co-inspired by their grandad’s store back in Toronto long ago. So this will be very special.” A.C.T. Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon said, “I am thrilled to be bringing Ins Choi, as playwright and actor, in his beautifully crafted and deeply personal prodigal son story Kim’s Convenience to A.C.T.” A.C.T. will present Our Store, Your Story, a photo and essay series that features San Francisco immigrant family-owned businesses, alongside showings. A revamped pre- and post-show party celebrating LGBTQ pride within the theater community will be held on Wednesday, October 8, and an aftershow Q&A session with actors and artists will take place on September 30, October 5 and October 8. Kim’s Convenience is directed by Weyni Mengesha. The cast includes Ins Choi as Appa, Esther Chung as Umma, Ryan Jinn as Jung and Kelly Seo as Janet. articles.text: Paul McCartney: Photographs 1963–64: Eyes of the Storm, currently on view at Legion of Honor in San Francisco, has been extended through October 5. The never-before-seen exhibition drew more than 100,000 visitors. The exhibition includes more than 250 of McCartney’s personal captures as well as video clips, archival materials and more that offer a behind-thescenes look at the meteoric rise of one of the world’s most celebrated and popular bands. Images span December 1963 through February 1964 and chronicle the Beatles’ journey to megastardom. Photographs were taken by McCartney with a single-lens reflex camera, which were introduced in the 1950’s as part of a new generation of handheld cameras. Sally Martin Katz, Legion of Honor Assistant Curator of Photography, said that McCartney acquired the camera in 1963 at a time “when many were experimenting with this newly popularized medium.” “The technology of the 35mm handheld camera allowed for a spontaneity in picture-taking, leading to the emergence of a snapshot aesthetic that embraced imperfection,” Katz said. “McCartney’s pictures reflect this new spirit in photography, as well as the literal blur of travel that The Beatles were experiencing, rapidly moving from one place to another.” Katz added that the exhibition, which includes photographs printed for the first time, captures “Beatlemania in full force.” “They depict the frenzied crowds chasing the band down the New York City streets, for example, and the swarms of people greeting them at the Miami airport,” she said. “The Beatles were at the eye of the storm they created: thousands of eyes were looking to capture that storm, and McCartney, with his camera, returned their gazes.” Visit https://www.famsf.org/ exhibitions/paul-mccartney-photographs to learn more. articles.text: Exhibition leaves museum Sept. 14 Kunié Sugiura: Photopainting, an exhibition featuring over 60 works by Japanese American photoartist Kunie Sugiura, leaves the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) on September 14. Japanese native Sugiura pioneered a unique category of artistic expression by blending photography with painting, drawing and other mediums. She also experimented with the photogram technique, one of the earliest forms of photography dating back to 1839. Kunié Sugiura: Photopainting, her first survey exhibition in the U.S., features over 60 artworks spanning her sixty-decades long career. “Throughout her career, Kunié Sugiura has subverted traditional notions of photography, bravely bucking trends to produce a distinctive body of work that is unmistakably her own,” said Erin O’Toole, SFMOMA’s curator and head of photography. “Sugiura’s many experiments and explorations with the photographic medium upend our notions of what photography can be,” added SFMOMA Director Christopher Bedford. “We look forward to engaging our communities with KuniéSugiura’s art and are honored to open the first survey exhibition of her work in the U.S.” Sugiura moved to the U.S. in 1963 to study at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago where she was a mentee of conceptual artist and photographer Kenneth Josephson. A major retrospective of her art was on display at the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum in 2018. From 1986 to 2008 she produced a column entitled “New York Report,” in which she reviewed gallery and museum exhibitions, for the Japanese-language magazine Bijutsu Techo. “I am very happy I found a way of life that has interested me and has kept my focus for so long,” Sugiura said in an interview with Cristina Chan, SFMOMA’s Managing Editor. “Over my career, I have had a few people and audiences who have supported my art. This time, I feel like more people are understanding my ideas and art.” Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/kunie-sugiura-photopainting/ to learn more. Kunié Sugiura

articles.text: In 1946, with London still marked by the Blitz, a letter arrived from a small island in the Channel. It draws writer Juliet Ashton into a world shaped by occupation, loss, and an unlikely book club: The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society. Juliet, played with quiet strength by Lily James, is a novelist whose own life has been scarred by the war. Encouraged by her editor Sidney Stark (Matthew Goode), she sets out to write about the solace books provide. The timing proves uncanny: a farmer from Guernsey, Dawsey Adams (Michiel Huisman), reaches out seeking a volume she might help him find. In his letter, he mentions the society, a group formed during the German occupation that survived on reading, and on each other. Curious, Juliet travels to Guernsey. What she imagines will be a quick visit turns into something else entirely. The island’s beauty hides darker memories, and the society’s eccentric name conceals a tragic story waiting to be told. At first, she observes as a guest, reading to the members at their gatherings and listening as they recall the war years. But soon, her connection deepens. Dawsey, kind and steady, emerges as more than just a correspondent. The bond between them quietly complicates Juliet’s engagement to an Lily James and Michiel Huisman in The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society American officer, Mark Reynolds (Glen Powell). Director Mike Newell, known for films like Four Weddings and a Funeral, leans into period detail, the bombed-out streets of London, the windswept coast of Guernsey, while letting the human story take center stage. The film shifts between present and wartime flashbacks, weaving together memory, resilience, and the way books helped sustain a community under occupation. If the plot sometimes feels familiar, its strength lies in the sincerity of its characters and the charm of its ensemble cast. Tom Courtenay, as the society’s elder statesman, adds gravitas, while Penelope Wilton gives a performance edged with grief and steel. Ultimately, Guernsey is less about mystery than about belonging. Juliet arrives searching for a story and finds, instead, a home among people who have endured loss yet cling to love, friendship, and the written word. Its conclusion is tender and satisfying, a reminder that even in the shadow of war, stories, and the communities built around them, can carry us forward. articles.text: There is a side story to everything. When I was teaching in the San Francisco public schools, kids wanted me to teach them rap. I responded that rap was something they could do on their own. They needed to explore the world, and music was the best way to do it. Every one of my students learned to read music with proficiency, sing the music of many lands and understand their cultures, recognize all the instruments of the Orchestra by sight and by sound, play the recorder with proficiency, and learned how to listen. These are just a few of the things that they learned – and they had fun doing it. Learning should be fun. In my opinion, music is one of the best ways to learn “cultural awareness“. At the same time that we become culturally aware, we learn geography among many other things. Why are different cultures attracted to their representative music? Let’s take a quick tour around the world. Perhaps we should start with one of the most vilified peoples of our world. These are the Romany people. They are also known as gypsies and Zigeuner. When they left their land of origin, they brought with them enthusiasm for music. Where would Hungarian or Romanian music be without the Zigeuner? Their musical voice was the violin and the cymbalom. When they went to Spain, flamenco music flourished and became the most characteristic music of the Iberian peninsula. The guitar was the voice of flamenco. articles.text: Few films capture the magic of childhood summers as vividly as The Sandlot. Released in 1993 but set in the summer of 1962, it is less about baseball than about belonging, friendship and the timeless rituals of growing up. Scottie Smalls (Tom Guiry), 13, is the awkward new kid who has just moved with his mom (Karen Allen) and stepdad (Denis Leary) to the San Fernando Valley. Encouraged to make friends, he stumbles onto a dusty sandlot where a group of neighborhood boys spend their days playing ball. Smalls can barely throw or catch, but team leader Benny Rodriguez (Mike Vitar) takes him under his wing. By summer’s end, the game has given Smalls more than skills. It has given him a place in the world. The boys’ universe revolves around the field, but their imaginations reach far beyond it. A snarling dog known only as “the Beast” guards the junkyard next door, swallowing every home-run ball that clears the fence. When Smalls accidentally offers up his stepdad’s prized Babe Ruth– signed ball, the team faces a quest that feels larger than life. The film’s humor is stitched together with moments anyone who grew up in a neighborhood pack will recognize: the first crush (Squints and lifeguard Wendy Peffercorn), tall tales told under streetlights, long afternoons that feel endless until school looms again. These vignettes make The Sandlot as much a memory piece as a sports film. articles.text: If your dog pulls on the leash, you’re not alone. It’s probably the number one thing people complain to me about. Puppies might learn “heel” pretty quickly with treats, but once they hit about six months — what I like to call the raptor phase — everything changes. Suddenly every smell, every squirrel, every blowing leaf is more exciting than you, and walking feels like being dragged behind a sled. So, what do you do? First, get the right gear. If your dog is pulling hard on a flat collar, swap it out. A front-clip harness — like the PetSafe Easy Walk — works well because it gently turns the dog back toward you instead of letting them dig in. Don’t bother with back-clip harnesses; those just give your dog more leverage. Some folks like the Gentle Leader, which goes over the muzzle. It can work wonders, but you have to be gentle with it. Don’t yank — that can hurt. Next, the leash. Keep it simple: a plain six-foot nylon, leather or biothane leash. No retractables, no bungees. Those teach dogs to lean into the tension, which makes pulling worse. Now, here’s the trick I use all the time: Mike Wombacher’s “Pay Attention Exercise.” It doesn’t take treats, just a bit of focus. Put your dog on your left, hold the leash in your right, and let a little loop cross your body. Start walking with purpose. Then, without warning, turn sharply away from your dog. The leash will tighten for just a second and the dog will have to catch up. As soon as they do, gather the loop, keep moving, and then turn again. Praise when they follow on a loose leash. The key here is pace. Don’t dawdle. Keep your feet moving and make your dog pay attention to you, not the other way around. If you’re using a Gentle Leader, give it a split second longer before the turn so you’re not snapping the dog’s neck. Most dogs figure this out after a few turns, sometimes even in the first session. It’s not magic, but it works — especially if you stay consistent. Pair the right tool with this exercise, and those exhausting, frustrating walks start to feel a lot calmer. Before long, it won’t be you following your dog, it’ll be your dog following you. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. The key here is pace. Don’t dawdle. Keep your feet moving and make your dog pay attention to you, not the other way around. If you’re using a Gentle Leader, give it a split second longer before the turn so you’re not snapping the dog’s neck. Most dogs figure this out after a few turns, sometimes even in the first session. It’s not magic, but it works — especially if you stay consistent. Pair the right tool with this exercise, and those exhausting, frustrating walks start to feel a lot calmer. Before long, it won’t be you following your dog, it’ll be your dog following you. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. The space is dedicated to church member Judy Wright’s late husband, Bob, who died in 2024. Wright, along with her daughter Lisa Fuller, church members Paul Schroeder and Suzie Skugstad, and many volunteers helped bring the garden to life. Much of the inspiration came from Sonja ten Grotenhuis, a church member who will attend Boston University this fall. Sonja created the garden as her Girl Scout Gold Award project, which requires more than 80 hours of work. With donations from church members and friends, and Schroeder’s heavy labor removing a concrete wall, the garden was transformed from a patch of weeds into a peaceful retreat. “Bob loved labyrinths,” Wright told the walkers. “This was the perfect way to honor him.” Sonja explained that the labyrinth and fountain are meant to bring nature into people’s lives and encourage reflection. She and Skugstad selected the stone for the fountain, while new benches and tree lights make the space welcoming both day and night. Like all Gold Award projects, Sonja said, the garden is designed to have a lasting community impact. The space is open to the public for quiet meditation and contemplation. Before heading to the garden, walkers heard about the church’s long history. Founded as the Piedmont Sunday School in 1900, it became the Piedmont Community Church in 1912. In the early 1980’s as a graduate student in Berkeley I would often make forays to the wine country to explore the fascinating new world of wine I was discovering. One of my most memorable early trips was prompted by an issue of Robert Parker’s wine magazine where he listed California’s greatest Pinot Noir producers. One winery that received special acclaim was Kent Rasmussen Winery in the Carneros region. It was there in that wild, remote wind-swept region that I first tasted great Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. (And also met a life-long friend.) In those days Carneros was the up-and-coming area for Pinot and Chardonnay. In the years since then other regions have captured some of the attention away from Carneros. The Russian River showed it was capable of world class Pinot Noir, then the Santa Lucia Highlands came into vogue. The high elevation vineyards in the Sonoma Coast region also gained notoriety. But the world’s attention seems to be returning to Carneros. Driving through Carneros recently there was a hive of activity and numerous new wineries I had never heard of in addition to some high-end resorts and restaurants that dot the landscape. Los Carneros AVA is an American Viticulture Area that spans across parts of Napa and Sonoma counties. It is known for its relatively cooler temperatures due to the marine fog and breezes coming in off San Pablo Bay. It is unique among American appellations in that it spans both Napa and Sonoma counties. Carneros is composed of a series of low rolling hills that sit above the San Pablo Bay and beneath Mount Veeder. The soils are predominantly sandy loam over clay. Because of the cooling influence of the Bay and regular fog and ocean breezes, Carneros is widely considered to be “Napa’s Burgundy” as Pinot Noir and Chardonnay thrive here. It could also be called “Napa’s Champagne” because multiple sparkling houses have set up shop here and produce truly world-class sparkling wine. I have known of the Cuvaison brand for many years but until recently I have never had the chance to visit the winery. Founded in 1969, Cuvaison is one of the pioneering wineries that helped put Napa Valley onto the global stage. In 1979 Cuvaison was acquired by the Schmidheiny family of Switzerland who still own the winery today. The Schmidheiny family cemented Cuvaison’s focus on Chardonnay and Pinot Noir by acquiring 400 acres of land north of San Pablo Bay on the Napa side of Carneros. In 2009 Cuvaison built a new 32,000 square foot winery. Steve Rogstad has been the head winemaker since 2002. In 2016 Dan Zepponi was named president and CEO of Cuvaison. Dan grew up in the wine industry as his father was co-founder of ZD winery. Dan graciously offered his time to guide me through a flight of the Cuvaison current releases. Sustainability and concern for the environment are core values for Cuvaison and there is a care and thoughtfulness evident in the layout of the winery and vineyards. The high-ceilinged glass-walled tasting room is bright and airy and sits on a hilltop with a stunning panoramic view of the vineyards and a beautiful reservoir. articles.text: BBQ Without Borders returned to the Oakland Museum of California earlier this month. Their event on August 2 was presented by the organization No Immigrants No Spice (NINS), and was a celebration of food and an affirmation of the often unacknowledged contributions of immigrant communities to the nation’s cultural richness and social fabric. “In a time when the narratives around immigration are often distorted, BBQ Without Borders offers a tangible space with a delicious counter-narrative,” said Dr. Vibha Gupta, a Piedmont resident and founder of No Immigrants No Spice. “We believe that by coming together over food, we can bridge divides, celebrate the cultural richness immigrants bring, and directly support those who are building our communities from the ground up.” This year’s event, themed “Toward A Greener Future,” looked to highlight the economic and cultural impact of immigrants. The food tents this year provided a culinary journey, with an array of flavors from a celebrated lineup of Bay Area immigrant chefs, including: • Anthony Salguero of Popoca: Bringing Salvadoran-inspired delights to the forefront. • Maria Marquez of Tacos Mama Cuca: Offering traditional and modern Mexican flavors from Sonora. • Cafe Colucci: Serving up renowned Ethiopian cuisine and seasonings. • Third Culture Bakery: Sweet Indonesian and Taiwanese inspired desserts from the bakery behind the Mochi Muffin. Beyond the mouth-watering food, BBQ Without Borders raised over $25,000 for the East Bay immigrant community, channeled through The Unity Council, an Oakland non-profit. The event also featured live music, dance, and a Silent Auction with artwork and photography. “What we have here today is the America I want to live in. Thank you for being here,” Gupta told the crowd. NINS is keeping its resilience fund open for donations until September 1. pages.text: Wednesday, August 20, 2025 29 BBQ Without Borders celebrates immigrant cuisine at Oakland Museum By Tony Simons BBQ Without Borders returned to the Oakland Museum of California earlier this month. Their event on August 2 was presented by the organization No Immigrants No Spice (NINS), and was a celebration of food and an affirmation of the often unacknowledged contributions of immigrant communities to the nation’s cultural richness and social fabric. “In a time when the narratives around immigration are often distorted, BBQ Without Borders offers a tangible space with a delicious counter-narrative,” said Dr. Vibha Gupta, a Piedmont resident and founder of No Immigrants No Spice. “We believe that by coming together over food, we can bridge divides, celebrate the cultural richness immigrants bring, and directly support those who are building our communities from the ground up.” This year’s event, themed “Toward A Greener Future,” looked to highlight the economic and cultural impact of immigrants. The food tents this year provided a culinary journey, with an array of flavors from a celebrated lineup of Bay Area immigrant chefs, including: • Anthony Salguero of Popoca: Bringing Salvadoran-inspired delights to the forefront. • Maria Marquez of Tacos Mama Cuca: Offering traditional and modern Mexican flavors from Sonora. • Cafe Colucci: Serving up renowned Ethiopian cuisine and seasonings. • Third Culture Bakery: Sweet Indonesian and Taiwanese inspired desserts from the bakery behind the Mochi Muffin. Beyond the mouth-watering food, BBQ Without Borders raised over $25,000 for the East Bay immigrant community, channeled through The Unity Council, an Oakland non-profit. The event also featured live music, dance, and a Silent Auction with artwork and photography. “What we have here today is the America I want to live in. Thank you for being here,” Gupta told the crowd. NINS is keeping its resilience fund open for donations until September 1. To donate, visit Photos by Scott Hoag A chef from Tacos Sinceros, led by Chef Sincere Justice, makes tacos at Oakland Museum on August 2. Displays in the museum plaza detail the history of the restaurants, along with the chefs behind the meals. A cook at Preeti’s Pani Puri Party, a live cooking demonstration and tasting with award-winning chef Preeti Mistry. noimmigrantsnospice.org/donate. All funds will be distributed in the form of micro-grants to immigrant families in Oakland, through NINS’ collaboration with The Unity Council. No Immigrants No Spice (NINS) is a non-profit organization that uses food as a vehicle to highlight the positive impact immigrants have on culture and society. Through events and initiatives like BBQ Without Borders, NINS aims to foster understanding, celebrate diversity, and provide critical support to immigrant communities, including the distribution of micro-grants. Learn more at https://noimmigrantsnospice.org/. This culinary force of cooks represented the Salvadorian restaurant Popoca, led by Chef Anthony Salguero.
